{{Short description|Conic curves associated with a triangle}}
In [[Modern triangle geometry|triangle geometry]], the '''Kiepert conics''' are two special [[conic]]s associated with the reference triangle. One of them is a [[hyperbola]], called the '''Kiepert hyperbola''' and the other is a [[parabola]], called the '''Kiepert parabola'''. The Kiepert conics are defined as follows:
:If the three triangles <math>A^\prime BC</math>, <math>AB^\prime C</math> and <math>ABC^\prime</math>, constructed on the sides of a triangle <math>ABC</math> as bases, are similar, isosceles and similarly situated, then the triangles <math>ABC</math> and <math>A^\prime B^\prime C^\prime</math> are in [[Perspective (geometry)|perspective]]. As the base angle of the isosceles triangles varies between <math>-\pi/2</math> and <math>\pi/2</math>, the [[Locus (mathematics)|locus]] of the [[center of perspectivity]] of the triangles <math>ABC</math> and  <math>A^\prime B^\prime C^\prime</math> is a hyperbola called the Kiepert hyperbola and the [[Envelope (mathematics)|envelope]] of their [[axis of perspectivity]] is a parabola called the Kiepert parabola.

It has been proved that the Kiepert hyperbola is the hyperbola passing through the vertices, the [[centroid]] and the [[orthocenter]] of the reference triangle and the Kiepert parabola is the parabola [[inconic|inscribed]] in the reference triangle having the [[Euler line]] as [[Directrix (conic section)|directrix]] and the [[triangle center]] X<sub>110</sub> as [[Focus (geometry)|focus]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kimberling, C. |title=X(110)=Focus of Kiepert Parabola |url=http://faculty.evansville.edu/ck6/encyclopedia/ETC.html#X110. |website=Encyclopedia of Triangle Centers |access-date=4 February 2022}}</ref> The following quote from a paper by R. H. Eddy and R. Fritsch is enough testimony to establish the importance of the Kiepert conics in the study of triangle geometry:<ref name="Eddy">{{cite journal |last1=Eddy |first1=R. H. |last2=Fritsch |first2=R. |title=The Conics of Ludwig Kiepert: A Comprehensive Lesson in the Geometry of the Triangle |journal=Math. Mag. |date=1994 |volume=67 |issue=3 |pages=188–205|doi=10.1080/0025570X.1994.11996212 }}</ref>
:"If a visitor from Mars desired to learn the geometry of the triangle but could stay in the earth's relatively dense atmosphere only long enough for a single lesson, earthling mathematicians would, no doubt, be hard-pressed to meet this request. In this paper, we believe that we have an optimum solution to the problem. The Kiepert conics ...."

==Kiepert hyperbola==
The Kiepert hyperbola was discovered by [[Friedrich Wilhelm August Ludwig Kiepert|Ludvig Kiepert]] while investigating the solution of the following problem proposed by [[Emile Lemoine]] in 1868: "Construct a triangle, given the peaks of the equilateral triangles constructed on the sides." A solution to the problem was published by [[Friedrich Wilhelm August Ludwig Kiepert|Ludvig Kiepert]] in 1869 and the solution contained a remark which effectively stated the locus definition of the Kiepert hyperbola alluded to earlier.<ref name="Eddy"/>

===Basic facts===
Let <math>a, b, c</math> be the side lengths and <math>A,B,C</math> the vertex angles of the reference triangle <math>ABC</math>.
====Equation====
The equation of the Kiepert hyperbola in barycentric coordinates <math>x:y:z</math> is

:<math>\frac{b^2-c^2}{x}+\frac{c^2-a^2}{y}+\frac{a^2-b^2}{z}=0.</math>

====Center, asymptotes====
*The centre of the Kiepert hyperbola is the triangle center X(115).  The barycentric coordinates of the center are

:<math>(b^2-c^2)^2 : (c^2-a^2)^2 : (a^2-b^2)^2</math>.

*The asymptotes of the Kiepert hyperbola are the [[Simson line]]s of the intersections of the [[Brocard axis]] with the [[circumcircle]]. 
*The Kiepert hyperbola is a [[rectangular hyperbola]] and hence its eccentricity is <math>\sqrt{2}</math>.

===Properties===
#The center of the Kiepert hyperbola lies on the [[nine-point circle]]. The center is the midpoint of the [[line segment]] joining the isogonic centers of triangle <math>ABC</math> which are the triangle centers X(13) and X(14) in the [[Encyclopedia of Triangle Centers]].
#The image of the Kiepert hyperbola under the [[Isogonal conjugate|isogonal transformation]] is the [[Brocard axis]] of triangle <math>ABC</math> which is the line joining the [[symmedian point]] and the [[circumcenter]].
#Let <math>P</math> be a point in the plane of a nonequilateral triangle <math>ABC</math> and let <math>p</math> be the trilinear polar of <math>P</math> with respect to <math>ABC</math>. The locus of the points <math>P</math> such that <math>p</math> is perpendicular to the Euler line of <math>ABC</math> is the Kiepert hyperbola.

==Kiepert parabola==
The Kiepert parabola was first studied in 1888 by a German mathematics teacher Augustus Artzt in a "school program".<ref name="Eddy"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sharp, J. |title=Artzt parabolas of a triangle |journal=The Mathematical Gazette |date=2015 |volume=99 |issue=546 |pages=444–463 |doi=10.1017/mag.2015.81|s2cid=123814409 }}</ref>

===Basic facts===
*The equation of the Kiepert parabola in barycentric coordinates <math>x:y:z</math> is

::<math>f^2x^2+g^2y^2+h^2z^2 - 2fgxy - 2ghyz - 2 hfzx=0</math> <br />where<br /><math>f=(b^2-c^2)/a, g=(c^2-a^2)/b, h=(a^2-b^2)/c</math>.

*The focus of the Kiepert parabola is the triangle center X(110). The barycentric coordinates of the focus are

::<math>a^2/(b^2-c^2) : b^2/(c^2-a^2) : c^2/(a^2-b^2)</math>

*The directrix of the Kiepert parabola is the Euler line of triangle <math>ABC</math>.
